claim: Antidepressants collectively account for one of the most prescribed medications.
source: Antidepressants are the first-line treatment for major depressive disorder (MDD), collectively accounting for one of the most prescribed medications (Brody and Gu, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brody and Gu, 2020

claim: Less than 50% of patients respond to first trial antidepressant treatment.
source: However, response to antidepressant treatment is variable with less than 50% of patients responding to first trial, and up to 40% with no clinical response after two or more trials (Cipriani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cipriani et al., 2018

claim: Up to 40% of patients have no clinical response after two or more antidepressant trials.
source: However, response to antidepressant treatment is variable with less than 50% of patients responding to first trial, and up to 40% with no clinical response after two or more trials (Cipriani et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cipriani et al., 2018

claim: Enhancement of monoamine function can be observed within hours after antidepressant drug administration.
source: Importantly, although the enhancement of monoamine function, in particular serotonin, can be observed within hours after antidepressant drug administration, clinical improvements are not observed until days or weeks following antidepressant treatment initiation (Harmer et al., 2017; Ross and Renyi, 1969; Vetulani and Sulser, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harmer et al., 2017; Ross and Renyi, 1969; Vetulani and Sulser, 1975

claim: Clinical improvements are not observed until days or weeks following antidepressant treatment initiation.
source: Importantly, although the enhancement of monoamine function, in particular serotonin, can be observed within hours after antidepressant drug administration, clinical improvements are not observed until days or weeks following antidepressant treatment initiation (Harmer et al., 2017; Ross and Renyi, 1969; Vetulani and Sulser, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harmer et al., 2017; Ross and Renyi, 1969; Vetulani and Sulser, 1975

claim: The glutamatergic system is believed to be the target of rapid acting antidepressants.
source: However, given the delayed clinical response other neurotransmitter systems have been gaining interest in depression; particularly the glutamatergic system, which is believed to be the target of rapid acting antidepressants (Berman et al., 2000; Duman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berman et al., 2000; Duman, 2018

claim: Monoaminergic antidepressants may act by modulating the glutamatergic system.
source: Moreover, recent evidence suggest that monoaminergic antidepressants may act by modulating the glutamatergic system, although it is still unclear through what molecular mechanisms (Bonanno et al., 2005; Musazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bonanno et al., 2005; Musazzi et al., 2013

claim: SNORD90 was the only snoRNA consistently up-regulated after antidepressant treatment in subjects who responded to treatment across all three independent cohorts.
source: In particular, SNORD90 was the only snoRNA that was consistently up-regulated after antidepressant treatment in subjects who responded to treatment across all three independent cohorts (Figure 1B, Supplementary files 1–3 & Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data from three independent clinical cohorts shown in Figure 1B and supplementary files

claim: SNORD90 is up-regulated in both neuronal and non-neuronal nuclei fractions in individuals with depression treated with antidepressants.
source: In both the neuronal and non-neuronal nuclei fractions we observed the same pattern of expression as in bulk tissue, where SNORD90 was up-regulated in individuals with depression that were actively treated with antidepressants at the time of death (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by FANS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Antidepressants do not up-regulate SNORD90 in a cell-type specific manner.
source: These results suggest that antidepressants do not up-regulate SNORD90 in a cell-type specific manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SNORD90 is up-regulated in both neuronal and non-neuronal nuclei fractions

claim: Snord90 is up-regulated in the ACC of mice that underwent UCMS followed by antidepressant administration.
source: Similar to the results observed in humans, we observed a specific up-regulation of Snord90 in the ACC of mice that underwent the UCMS paradigm followed by antidepressant administration, whereas UCMS or antidepressant administration alone did not alter the expression of Snord90 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data from UCMS mouse model shown in Figure 1D

claim: UCMS or antidepressant administration alone did not alter the expression of Snord90.
source: Similar to the results observed in humans, we observed a specific up-regulation of Snord90 in the ACC of mice that underwent the UCMS paradigm followed by antidepressant administration, whereas UCMS or antidepressant administration alone did not alter the expression of Snord90 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by data from UCMS mouse model shown in Figure 1D

claim: SNORD90 expression is up-regulated exclusively by antidepressant drugs in human neuronal cultures.
source: We observed that SNORD90 expression was up-regulated exclusively by antidepressant drugs, while other treatments did not significantly alter SNORD90 expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by data from human neuronal cultures treated with various psychotropic drugs shown in Figure 1E

claim: Snord90 over-expression in mouse cg1/2 increased the amount of time spent in the open arm of the elevated plus maze.
source: Snord90 over-expression increased the amount of time spent in the open arm and decreased the amount of time spent in the closed arm of the elevated plus maze (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Snord90 over-expression in mouse cg1/2 decreased the amount of time spent in the closed arm of the elevated plus maze.
source: Snord90 over-expression increased the amount of time spent in the open arm and decreased the amount of time spent in the closed arm of the elevated plus maze (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Snord90 over-expression in mouse cg1/2 increased time spent grooming in the splash test.
source: Moreover, Snord90 over-expression increased time spent grooming after splashing with 10% sucrose solution (Figure 2D) and increased time spent struggling in the tail suspension test (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Snord90 over-expression in mouse cg1/2 increased time spent struggling in the tail suspension test.
source: Moreover, Snord90 over-expression increased time spent grooming after splashing with 10% sucrose solution (Figure 2D) and increased time spent struggling in the tail suspension test (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Over-expressing Snord90 levels in cg1/2 yielded decreased emotionality indicative of a decrease in anxiety-like and depressive-like behaviours.
source: Overall, our results consistently showed that over-expressing Snord90 levels in cg1/2 yielded decreased emotionality (Figure 2F) indicative of a decrease in anxiety-like and depressive-like behaviours.
evidence: Supported by integrated emotionality Z-score data shown in Figure 2F

claim: NRG3 is a growth factor that is part of the neuregulin family which is highly enriched in the brain.
source: NRG3 is a growth factor that is part of the neuregulin family which is highly enriched in the brain and has been previously associated with psychiatric phenotypes (Paterson et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paterson et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 1997

claim: NRG3 has been previously associated with psychiatric phenotypes.
source: NRG3 is a growth factor that is part of the neuregulin family which is highly enriched in the brain and has been previously associated with psychiatric phenotypes (Paterson et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paterson et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 1997

claim: There is a negative correlation between SNORD90 and NRG3 in human ACC, mouse ACC, and neuronal cultures.
source: We observed a negative correlation between SNORD90 and NRG3 in all three experimental contexts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), and interestingly, we observed the most significant differences in direction of fold-change between SNORD90 and NRG3 expression in groups with antidepressant drug exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F

claim: The most significant differences in direction of fold-change between SNORD90 and NRG3 expression occur in groups with antidepressant drug exposure.
source: We observed a negative correlation between SNORD90 and NRG3 in all three experimental contexts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), and interestingly, we observed the most significant differences in direction of fold-change between SNORD90 and NRG3 expression in groups with antidepressant drug exposure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–I

claim: Over-expressing SNORD90 resulted in approximately 50% decrease in NRG3 expression at both the mRNA and protein levels.
source: Over-expressing SNORD90 resulted in a~50% decrease in NRG3 expression at both the mRNA (Figure 3B) and protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data from human NPC culture shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Seed scramble and full scramble over-expression did not alter the expression of NRG3.
source: Seed scramble and full scramble over-expression did not alter the expression of NRG3, indicating the region of predicted complementarity between SNORD90 and NRG3 plays an important role in the ability of SNORD90 to down-regulate NRG3 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data from human NPC culture shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The region of predicted complementarity between SNORD90 and NRG3 plays an important role in the ability of SNORD90 to down-regulate NRG3.
source: Seed scramble and full scramble over-expression did not alter the expression of NRG3, indicating the region of predicted complementarity between SNORD90 and NRG3 plays an important role in the ability of SNORD90 to down-regulate NRG3 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that scrambled controls did not alter NRG3 expression

claim: SNORD90 knock-down by approximately 55% resulted in approximately 50% up-regulation of NRG3 expression.
source: SNORD90 knock-down by approximately 55% resulted in a~50% up-regulation of NRG3 expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by data from human NPC culture with ASO knock-down shown in Figure 3C

claim: Pre-NRG3 expression was not altered by SNORD90 over-expression or knock-down.
source: Given that our in-silico predictions indicate that SNORD90 is primarily interacting with intronic regions of pre-NRG3, we next investigated that expression of pre-NRG3 in the same experiments detailed above; however, pre-NRG3 expression was not altered by SNORD90 over-expression or knock-down (Figure 3—figure supplement 1S–T).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1S–T

claim: When each individual site was blocked, a partial rescue of NRG3 expression was observed.
source: Interestingly, when each individual site was blocked, we observed a partial rescue of NRG3 expression (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by data from target blocker experiments shown in Figure 3E

claim: Simultaneously blocking all three predicted sites was required for a complete rescue of the down-regulation effects of over-expressing SNORD90.
source: However, simultaneously blocking all three predicted sites was required for a complete rescue of the down-regulation effects of over-expressing SNORD90 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by data from target blocker experiments shown in Figure 3E

claim: SNORD90 directly down-regulates NRG3 expression through multiple interaction sites on intronic regions of pre-NRG3.
source: Together our data suggests that SNORD90 directly down-regulates NRG3 expression through multiple interaction sites on intronic regions of pre-NRG3.
evidence: Inferred from target blocker experiments and in silico predictions

claim: RBM15B is a key regulator of RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications by facilitating interactions with WTAP, which in turn binds to METTL3 forming a major m6A writer complex.
source: RBM15B is a key regulator of RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications by facilitating interactions with Wilms' tumor 1-associating protein (WTAP), which in turn binds to methyltransferase like 3 (METTL3) forming a major m6A writer complex (Patil et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patil et al., 2016

claim: SNORD90 displayed a significantly higher level of association to RBM15B compared to fibrillarin.
source: We observed a significantly higher level of association of SNORD90 to RBM15B compared to fibrillarin, whereas a canonically functioning snoRNA, SNORD44, displayed enrichment for fibrillarin IP (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RIP data shown in Figure 4A

claim: SNORD44 displayed enrichment for fibrillarin IP.
source: We observed a significantly higher level of association of SNORD90 to RBM15B compared to fibrillarin, whereas a canonically functioning snoRNA, SNORD44, displayed enrichment for fibrillarin IP (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RIP data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Over-expression of SNORD90 resulted in an increase in association of SNORD90 with RBM15B.
source: Furthermore, when we over-expressed SNORD90 we observed an increase in association of SNORD90 with RBM15B, compared to over-expression of a scrambled control (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RIP data following SNORD90 over-expression shown in Figure 4B

claim: SNORD90 over-expression did not increase association with fibrillarin.
source: We did not observe an increase of SNORD90 association with fibrillarin following SNORD90 over-expression, indicating that SNORD90 showed preference for interacting with RBM15B (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RIP data following SNORD90 over-expression shown in Figure 4B

claim: SNORD90 showed preference for interacting with RBM15B.
source: We did not observe an increase of SNORD90 association with fibrillarin following SNORD90 over-expression, indicating that SNORD90 showed preference for interacting with RBM15B (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SNORD90 over-expression increased association with RBM15B but not fibrillarin

claim: SNORD90 over-expression resulted in an increase of m6A abundance on both pre-NRG3 and NRG3.
source: We observed an increase of m6A abundance on both pre-NRG3 and NRG3, following SNORD90 over-expression, whereas seed scramble and full scramble over-expression did not alter m6A abundance (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by m6A-RIP data shown in Figure 4C–E

claim: Seed scramble and full scramble over-expression did not alter m6A abundance on pre-NRG3 and NRG3.
source: We observed an increase of m6A abundance on both pre-NRG3 and NRG3, following SNORD90 over-expression, whereas seed scramble and full scramble over-expression did not alter m6A abundance (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: Supported by m6A-RIP data shown in Figure 4C–E

claim: Introducing target blockers blunted the increase of m6A abundance on both NRG3 and pre-NRG3.
source: Furthermore, introducing target blockers blunted the increase of m6A abundance on both NRG3 and pre-NRG3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by m6A-RIP data with target blockers shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between m6A levels and expression of NRG3.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significant negative correlation between m6A levels and expression of NRG3, but this was not observed for pre-NRG3, which could possibly be explained by the fact that m6A-readers are primarily located in the cytoplasm, and thus would only recognize the m6A-modifications of the mature NRG3 transcript and promote its decay when it is shuttled out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 4D and F

claim: There is no significant correlation between m6A levels and expression of pre-NRG3.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significant negative correlation between m6A levels and expression of NRG3, but this was not observed for pre-NRG3, which could possibly be explained by the fact that m6A-readers are primarily located in the cytoplasm, and thus would only recognize the m6A-modifications of the mature NRG3 transcript and promote its decay when it is shuttled out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Supported by correlation data shown in Figure 4D and F

claim: M6A-readers are primarily located in the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, we observed a significant negative correlation between m6A levels and expression of NRG3, but this was not observed for pre-NRG3, which could possibly be explained by the fact that m6A-readers are primarily located in the cytoplasm, and thus would only recognize the m6A-modifications of the mature NRG3 transcript and promote its decay when it is shuttled out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about m6A-reader localization

claim: M6A modifications are added onto nascent pre-mRNA during transcription.
source: Ke et al., 2017 demonstrated that m6A modifications are added onto nascent pre-mRNA during transcription (Ke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ke et al., 2017

claim: M6A levels remain unchanged between nascent pre-mRNA and steady-state mRNA in the cytoplasm.
source: Moreover, m6A levels remain unchanged between nascent pre-mRNA and steady-state mRNA in the cytoplasm (Ke et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ke et al., 2017

claim: RBM15B knock-down followed by SNORD90 over-expression blunted the increase of m6A levels on pre-NRG3 and NRG3.
source: RBM15B knock-down followed by SNORD90 over-expression blunted the increase of m6A levels on pre-NRG3 and NRG3 (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by data from RBM15B knock-down experiments shown in Figure 4G–H

claim: RBM15B knock-down blunted the decrease of NRG3 expression following SNORD90 over-expression.
source: RBM15B knock-down also blunted the decrease of NRG3 expression following SNORD90 over-expression while pre-NRG3 levels were unaffected (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by data from RBM15B knock-down experiments shown in Figure 4G–H

claim: Pre-NRG3 levels were unaffected by RBM15B knock-down.
source: RBM15B knock-down also blunted the decrease of NRG3 expression following SNORD90 over-expression while pre-NRG3 levels were unaffected (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by data from RBM15B knock-down experiments shown in Figure 4G–H

claim: SNORD90 is guiding m6A modifications onto NRG3 at the pre-mRNA level, which are retained in the mRNA molecule.
source: Our results further support the findings from Ke et al., 2017, as it is possible that SNORD90 is guiding m6A modifications onto NRG3 at the pre-mRNA level, which are retained in the mRNA molecule (Figure 4D).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citation to Ke et al., 2017

claim: YTHDF2 knock-down displayed the most robust ability to blunt decreased NRG3 expression following SNORD90 over-expression.
source: Although knocking down YTHDF1, YTHDF2, and YTHDF3 all showed the ability to blunt decreased NRG3 expression following SNORD90 over-expression, YTHDF2 knock-down displayed the most robust ability to blunt this effect, recovering NRG3 expression to wild-type patterns (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data from m6A-reader knock-down experiments shown in Figure 5A

claim: Knock-down of YTHDC2 and YTHDC1 did not blunt the decrease of NRG3 expression after SNORD90 over-expression.
source: On the other hand, knock-down of YTHDC2 and YTHDC1 did not blunt the decrease of NRG3 expression after SNORD90 over-expression; displaying similar patterns of NRG3 expression to SNORD90 over-expression with a dsiRNA scramble control (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data from m6A-reader knock-down experiments shown in Figure 5A

claim: YTHDC1 knock-down resulted in a decrease of pre-NRG3 expression compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, YTHDC1 knock-down (the nuclear m6A-reader), resulted in a decrease of pre- NRG3 expression compared to wild-type, while knock-down of all other m6A-readers had no significant effect on pre-NRG3 expression levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by data from m6A-reader knock-down experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K

claim: Knock-down of all other m6A-readers had no significant effect on pre-NRG3 expression levels.
source: Interestingly, YTHDC1 knock-down (the nuclear m6A-reader), resulted in a decrease of pre- NRG3 expression compared to wild-type, while knock-down of all other m6A-readers had no significant effect on pre-NRG3 expression levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by data from m6A-reader knock-down experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K

claim: SNORD90 increases m6A abundance on pre-NRG3, which is retained onto mature NRG3 transcripts.
source: Together this evidence supports the hypothesis that (1) SNORD90 increases m6A abundance on pre-NRG3, which is retained onto mature NRG3 transcripts and (2) the increase in m6A abundance promotes YTHDF2 mediated NRG3 decay which occurs primarily in the cytoplasm (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including m6A-RIP and m6A-reader knock-down experiments

claim: The increase in m6A abundance promotes YTHDF2 mediated NRG3 decay which occurs primarily in the cytoplasm.
source: Together this evidence supports the hypothesis that (1) SNORD90 increases m6A abundance on pre-NRG3, which is retained onto mature NRG3 transcripts and (2) the increase in m6A abundance promotes YTHDF2 mediated NRG3 decay which occurs primarily in the cytoplasm (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including m6A-RIP and m6A-reader knock-down experiments

claim: Nrg3 has previously been shown to interact with syntaxin, disrupting SNARE complex formation in the presynaptic terminal, and inhibiting vesicle docking in mice.
source: Nrg3 has previously been shown to interact with syntaxin, disrupting SNARE complex formation in the presynaptic terminal, and inhibiting vesicle docking in mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018 and illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Nrg3 knock-out resulted in increased probability of glutamate release in mouse hippocampal neurons.
source: Nrg3 knock-out resulted in increased probability of glutamate release in mouse hippocampal neurons (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: Over-expression of Snord90 in mouse ACC resulted in down-regulation of Nrg3.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed successful over-expression of Snord90 and subsequent down-regulation of Nrg3 in mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from mouse ACC shown in Figure 6B

claim: Snord90 over-expression resulted in an increase in spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSC) frequency without any effect on sEPSC amplitude.
source: We observed an increase in spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSC) frequency following Snord90 over-expression without any effect on sEPSC amplitude (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recording data shown in Figure 5C–E

claim: The increase in glutamatergic neurotransmission is likely due to an increase in glutamate release probably resulting from Nrg3 pre-synaptic expression and effect on SNARE complex.
source: This increase in glutamatergic neurotransmission is likely due to an increase in glutamate release probably resulting from Nrg3 pre-synaptic expression and effect on SNARE complex (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: SNORD90-mediated down-regulation of NRG3 has implications in glutamate neurotransmission, which translates to behavioral changes such as anxiolytic and anti-depressive-like behaviors.
source: Together this indicates that SNORD90-mediated down-regulation of NRG3 has implications in glutamate neurotransmission, which translates to behavioral changes such as anxiolytic and anti-depressive-like behaviors (Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results including behavioral tests and electrophysiology

claim: Serotonin signaling via binding to serotonin receptors has been shown to be linked with chromatin remodeling thereby modulating gene expression.
source: Serotonin signaling via binding to serotonin receptors has been shown to be linked with chromatin remodeling thereby modulating gene expression (Holloway and González-Maeso, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holloway and González-Maeso, 2015

claim: Serotonin can modify histones, specifically the glutamine at the Q5 site in histone H3.
source: Accordingly, a recent study points to the ability of serotonin to modify histones. Specifically, the glutamine at the Q5 site in histone H3 can be modified by serotonin which promotes the recruitment of transcription factor II D (TFIID) and promotes gene expression (Farrelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrelly et al., 2019

claim: Serotonin modification of histone H3 promotes the recruitment of transcription factor II D (TFIID) and promotes gene expression.
source: Accordingly, a recent study points to the ability of serotonin to modify histones. Specifically, the glutamine at the Q5 site in histone H3 can be modified by serotonin which promotes the recruitment of transcription factor II D (TFIID) and promotes gene expression (Farrelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farrelly et al., 2019

claim: NRG3 is almost exclusively expressed in the central nervous system with the highest expression in the anterior cingulate and frontal cortex.
source: Additionally, according to the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, NRG3 is almost exclusively expressed in the central nervous system with the highest expression in the anterior cingulate and frontal cortex; NRG3 also displays the strongest specificity to the central nervous system as compared to the other neuregulin paralogs (Avramopoulos, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avramopoulos, 2018 and GTEx project data

claim: NRG3 displays the strongest specificity to the central nervous system as compared to the other neuregulin paralogs.
source: Additionally, according to the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project, NRG3 is almost exclusively expressed in the central nervous system with the highest expression in the anterior cingulate and frontal cortex; NRG3 also displays the strongest specificity to the central nervous system as compared to the other neuregulin paralogs (Avramopoulos, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avramopoulos, 2018 and GTEx project data

claim: NRG3 has been associated with several psychiatric illnesses, primarily schizophrenia but also MDD and bipolar disorder.
source: NRG3 has been associated with several psychiatric illnesses, primarily schizophrenia but also MDD and bipolar disorder; however, the functional relevance of NRG3 remains poorly understood (Paterson et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2009; Kao et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paterson et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2009; Kao et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2008

claim: NRG3 acts in a cell-autonomous manner specifically in pyramidal neurons and not by activating ERBB4 receptors.
source: A more recent study suggested that NRG3 acts in a cell-autonomous manner specifically in pyramidal neurons and not by activating ERBB4 receptors (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: NRG3 interacts with syntaxin 1 at the SNARE domain, resulting in the inhibition of SNARE-complex formation preventing vesicle docking and reducing glutamate release.
source: They propose that NRG3 interacts with syntaxin 1(specially at the SNARE domain), at the pre-synaptic terminal, resulting in the inhibition of SNARE-complex formation preventing vesicle docking and reducing glutamate release (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: Antidepressant treatment is linked to an up-regulation of SNORD90.
source: In summary, our proposed model suggests that antidepressant treatment is linked to an up-regulation of SNORD90, which in turn recruits the m6A-writer complex and guides this complex onto pre-NRG3 increasing the abundance of m6A modifications which is further retained onto the mature NRG3 transcript.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results across clinical cohorts and model systems

claim: SNORD90 recruits the m6A-writer complex and guides this complex onto pre-NRG3 increasing the abundance of m6A modifications.
source: In summary, our proposed model suggests that antidepressant treatment is linked to an up-regulation of SNORD90, which in turn recruits the m6A-writer complex and guides this complex onto pre-NRG3 increasing the abundance of m6A modifications which is further retained onto the mature NRG3 transcript.
evidence: Inferred from RIP and m6A-RIP experimental results

claim: The greater abundance of m6A modifications on NRG3 is recognized by the m6A-reader, YTHDF2, which mediates NRG3 decay.
source: In turn, the greater abundance of m6A modifications on NRG3 is recognized by the m6A-reader, YTHDF2, which mediates NRG3 decay.
evidence: Inferred from m6A-reader knock-down experimental results

claim: The reduction in NRG3 levels is associated with an increase in glutamatergic signaling which contributes to antidepressant response.
source: This reduction in NRG3 levels is associated with an increase in glutamatergic signaling which, we believe, contributes to antidepressant response.
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiology and behavioral experimental results

claim: Drugs targeting the glutamatergic system, in particular ketamine, result in rapid alleviation of MDD symptoms.
source: The glutamatergic system has become of great interest in antidepressant therapeutics research since drugs targeting this system, in particular ketamine, results in rapid alleviation of MDD symptoms.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about ketamine's rapid antidepressant effects

claim: Monoaminergic antidepressants have associative effects on the glutamatergic system.
source: It has been repeatedly shown that monoaminergic antidepressants have associative effects on the glutamatergic system, however the exact molecular mechanistic link between the two system has remained unknown (Musazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Musazzi et al., 2013

claim: SnoRNAs play a role in antidepressant treatment response.
source: Our findings suggest that snoRNAs play a role in antidepressant treatment response and provides a molecular link between monoaminergic targeting antidepressants to implications to the glutamatergic system.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental results presented in the study

claim: This study provides a molecular link between monoaminergic targeting antidepressants and the glutamatergic system.
source: Our findings suggest that snoRNAs play a role in antidepressant treatment response and provides a molecular link between monoaminergic targeting antidepressants to implications to the glutamatergic system.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental results presented in the study

claim: The disinhibition hypothesis suggests that ketamine may be preferentially inhibiting NMDA receptors located on GABAergic interneurons thus disinhibiting excitatory pyramidal neurons leading to an enhancement of glutamatergic neurotransmission.
source: Among these theories, the disinhibition hypothesis suggests that ketamine may be preferentially inhibiting NMDA receptors located on GABAergic interneurons thus disinhibiting excitatory pyramidal neurons leading to an enhancement of glutamatergic neurotransmission.
evidence: Draws from established theories about ketamine's mechanism of action

claim: An increase in glutamatergic neurotransmission is associated with a response to monoaminergic-acting antidepressant.
source: Our findings support the notion that the monoamine system may be playing more of a modularly role to the glutamatergic system to achieve an antidepressant outcome; in particular we observed that an increase in glutamatergic neurotransmission is associated with a response to monoaminergic-acting antidepressant.
evidence: Inferred from electrophysiology and behavioral experimental results

claim: SnoRNAs play a role in m6A modifications which ultimately has regulatory roles in the stability of mRNA.
source: We are the first to propose that snoRNAs play a role in m6A modifications which ultimately has regulatory roles in the stability of mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive experimental results presented in the study
